The dominant trend is toward localized, scope-limited ceasefires, not a nationwide one. The Oleshky humanitarian pause is a real signal: both governments confirmed it, it actually took effect, and the aid mission reportedly worked. That is momentum — but it is momentum in micro-arrangements. The trajectory from one town to the entire front is not an extrapolation; it is a phase jump. The data show continuing deep strikes, drone and missile attacks, and frontline pressure in Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia. There is no deceleration signal in the actual violence that would support a nationwide halt by 31 December.

The diplomatic trend is more active than it was in the summer: the Kremlin says it is ready to resume trilateral talks in mid-November, Zelenskyy has signaled readiness for a full ceasefire or separate arrangements, and Rubio is talking about growing interest in a limited Black Sea ceasefire. But look at the direction of the proposals: energy truce, Black Sea truce, Oleshky-style humanitarian corridors. The slope is positive for limited ceasefires. The line for a joint nationwide ceasefire with a stated effective date remains flat. Russia rejected a ceasefire proposal as recently as late October. A two-month window with talks restarting mid-November is very short for the territorial, verification, and political issues that a nationwide ceasefire requires.

The most likely path is more local pauses, possible energy or maritime arrangements, and continued fighting elsewhere. A nationwide announcement would require an exogenous shock — heavy US pressure plus a Russian calculation that a short nationwide truce serves its interests — and I do not see that inflection point in the current rates of change. The Oleshky success could be a template, but templates scale slowly. If the mid-November talks produce a joint draft with monitoring and an explicit nationwide effective date, I would revise upward quickly. Without that, the trend line says no.

My prediction is NO: Russia and Ukraine will not jointly announce a nationwide ceasefire between 1 November and 31 December 2026. Probability range: 15 to 25 percent.

Before anyone tells me about Oleshky or the mid-November talks, let’s identify the reference class. We are asking whether two governments in an active, high-intensity interstate war with maximalist territorial aims will jointly announce a nationwide ceasefire inside a two-month window. The empirical base rate for this conflict is zero qualifying events since February 2022. Minsk II was limited to parts of Donbas, not nationwide. The May 2026 three-day truce was a humanitarian and prisoner-exchange pause that collapsed. The April 2026 Easter ceasefire was another temporary humanitarian arrangement. Oleshky is one city. So the base rate is not “peace talks are happening”; it is “full nationwide mutual ceasefire announcements happen very rarely in this war, especially within weeks of failed negotiations.”

The inside view has real positive signals: Zelenskyy said on October 25 that Ukraine is ready for a full ceasefire or separate agreements; the Kremlin says it is ready to resume trilateral talks in mid-November; the U.S. is pushing; and the local Oleshky ceasefire actually held well enough to complete a humanitarian mission. But those are weak adjustments against the base rate. Russia is still advancing near Dobropillya and striking Ukrainian infrastructure. Ukraine is still deep-striking Russian refining capacity. The core issues—territory, security guarantees, and verification—remain unresolved. A mid-November meeting leaves roughly six weeks to bridge them. In comparable wars, that is a tail event. The Oleshky precedent shows the parties can cooperate on narrow humanitarian tracks while avoiding the nationwide question.

I’d put central probability around 7 to 8 percent, with a range of 5 to 12 percent. I would move up if by mid-December both governments publicly endorse a U.S.- or OSCE-verified nationwide framework with an effective date. I would move down to 2 to 4 percent if Russia rejects a full ceasefire at the resuming talks or if talks slip into 2027. The strict resolution—joint official confirmation, nationwide scope, stated start date—cuts against counting holiday rhetoric or unilateral gestures. Base rate says no.

Council members, I would separate three things that are being blurred in this reporting: the resumption of talks, a monitoring framework, and an actual nationwide ceasefire. The Kremlin’s signal is real but narrow. France 24 and the Kyiv Independent both report that Moscow is ready to resume trilateral talks with Washington and Kyiv in mid-November, after November 4. That is a diplomatic opening, and it matters, but it is not itself a ceasefire. It is a decision to return to the table, not a decision to stop the shooting across the front.

The local picture is more encouraging than the national one, but only up to a point. The Oleshky humanitarian ceasefire appears to be holding, as AP and NPR reported, and that shows the parties can still implement a narrow, locally monitored arrangement when evacuation and practical incentives align. But Euronews quotes a former Ukrainian prime minister warning that this will not bring a wider truce, and I think that caution is well placed. A local evacuation pause in one city does not scale automatically to a thousand-kilometer front line. Meanwhile, the Kyiv Post reports that the energy ceasefire failed, and the Kremlin rejected an energy ceasefire proposal. That is a warning that even limited sectoral deals are fragile.

There is also a genuine technical track. The Wikipedia summary of the 2026 Geneva meetings says negotiators were nearing a full draft on ceasefire monitoring, and the Congressional Research Service notes that Zelensky had earlier called for a full ceasefire for the duration of negotiations. So the machinery for monitoring may be closer than the rhetoric suggests. But a monitoring draft is not implementation, and implementation requires enforcement, verification, and political cover on both sides. The Baidu summary captures the tension well: a ceasefire in 2026 is widely seen as highly probable, but a comprehensive peace agreement still faces enormous challenges. I would add that a nationwide ceasefire before the end of 2026 is a narrower proposition than a comprehensive peace deal, but it still requires Moscow and Kyiv to accept the same line, the same monitoring, and the same consequences for violations.

So my judgment is that the mid-November talks are likely to happen, and a monitoring framework may be close, but a full nationwide ceasefire taking hold before the end of 2026 remains uncertain and on the lower side of even odds. The Oleshky precedent is useful but not sufficient; the failed energy ceasefire is a cautionary counterexample. I would put the probability of a nationwide, comprehensive ceasefire taking hold before the end of 2026 at roughly thirty to forty-five percent. That is not a dismissal of the diplomatic track. It is a recognition that talks resuming is not the same as a ceasefire holding.

The first thing every linear forecaster in this room is going to do is look at the Oleshky ceasefire and the mid-November trilateral talks and draw a straight line to "deal by Christmas." That's the trap. This system doesn't move in straight lines — it moves through coupled feedback loops, and the loop that actually governs this question is the one nobody's drawing: the localized-success loop running against the territorial-status veto.

Here's the causal chain as I see it. The Oleshky humanitarian pause — brokered by Melania Trump, confirmed by both militaries — is real and it did work. That seeds a reinforcing loop: successful local cooperation → reduced mutual suspicion → appetite for the next increment. And you can see the increment being queued up: Rubio on October 31 flagging "growing interest" in a Black Sea ceasefire, Zelensky floating an energy-strike moratorium, the Kremlin saying it's ready to resume trilateral talks mid-November. So the machine is producing a staircase of limited deals. Good.

But now trace the second-order effect. The resolution explicitly excludes geographically limited arrangements and humanitarian pauses. So every one of these staircase steps — Oleshky, Black Sea, energy truce — is a non-event for this question. And here's the feedback that matters: each limited deal actually relieves pressure for the full one. It gives both capitals a deliverable to show Washington without touching territorial status. It's a pressure-relief valve. The staircase becomes a substitute for the breakthrough, not a path to it.

Then the veto loop. The single structural blocker is territorial status, and Russia is the veto player. The RBC reporting is explicit — Russia rejects ceasefire proposals. Why? Because a nationwide freeze locks the frontline where Russian forces are still grinding forward near Dobropillya and Zaporizhzhia, and Moscow's own internal logic says a ceasefire lets Ukraine rearm and regroup. That's a balancing loop that activates precisely at the moment you'd expect a nationwide announcement: the closer you get to a real freeze, the more Russia's incentive to refuse grows. The May 2026 three-day truce is the proof-of-concept — agreed, announced, and it unraveled within days. Both sides learned the wrong lesson: announcements are cheap, implementation is not, and announcing a nationwide ceasefire you can't hold is a reputational cost.

So what would have to happen to tip this? You'd need the territorial question to crack — a framework where Russia gets de facto control acknowledged and Ukraine gets security guarantees — inside a sixty-day window. The Paris Declaration and the US-led monitoring architecture exist on paper, but verification and territorial ratification are exactly the pieces that have blocked this for four years. Minsk is the cautionary tale: a signed, announced, comprehensive ceasefire that was structurally unimplementable. The system remembers that.

I'm not saying zero. The positive path is real: mid-November talks produce a framework, US pressure converges with a Russian desire to bank gains before winter, and both capitals jointly announce a nationwide ceasefire with a stated start date as a political deliverable — announcement, not implementation, which the resolution only requires. That's a genuine tail. But the balancing loops — Russia's rearmament fear, the absence of any territorial settlement, and the pressure-relief dynamic of the staircase — dominate inside a two-month window. The staircase keeps going; the summit doesn't get climbed.

What would move me up sharply: credible reporting that Moscow has dropped territorial preconditions, or that a verification mechanism has been agreed with a named start date. What would move me down: another failed trilateral round or a new Russian offensive push that hardens positions.

That is technically possible and would not need to hold in practice to resolve YES. But the failure modes are severe. Territorial status remains unresolved, security guarantees are unresolved, verification is not operational, and Russia has been reported to reject a ceasefire proposal even as Ukraine signals readiness. The Oleshky model does not scale: one city with a humanitarian corridor can be monitored by local commanders; a nationwide ceasefire requires a monitoring architecture, violation-response rules, and political cover on both sides. None of that exists at the required speed.

There is also a correlated-risk problem. Local ceasefire success can create an illusion of momentum, but it can also raise spoiler incentives. If Oleshky holds, hardliners on either side may escalate elsewhere to prove the pause is not a precedent. If it breaks, the talks lose their pilot case. Meanwhile the frontline is still active: Russian forces are pressing near Dobropillya, strikes continue, and the May 2026 three-day truce unraveled quickly. The historical base rate from Minsk and the Easter ceasefire is that ceasefires are announced more easily than they are implemented, but a joint nationwide announcement in a two-month window remains rare precisely because both sides need to sell it domestically as a win.

So I am not predicting zero. I am pricing a small but non-negligible tail. My central estimate is that the probability of a genuine joint nationwide ceasefire announcement between November 1 and December 31, 2026 is in the high single digits to low teens. The expected case is continued limited arrangements, resumed talks, and no nationwide joint announcement. I would raise my confidence sharply if a mid-November trilateral meeting produced a signed framework with a nationwide scope and effective date, or if both presidents scheduled simultaneous addresses. I would lower it further if Moscow formally rejects the proposal, talks slip past mid-November, or the Oleshky pause collapses.
